EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Executive Summary Zackary Mark is a student advocate at Sun Prairie West High School. He runs two independent projects: SPASD Student Voice (since January 2026), which brings student input to Sun Prairie Area School District leaders, and Sun Prairie ALPR (since July 2026), a plain-language community report on the police department's license plate reader cameras. What changed because students spoke up • District newsletters will go to every student, confirmed in writing on October 21. • Students sat on principal interviews and met the superintendent finalists, and a Student Senate restarted at Sun Prairie West. • Students helped write the weighted grades plan; it went to the Board on November 9, with a final vote expected late November. • Superintendent Dr. Reed backed a District-Wide Student Council ("I love this idea"); Patrick Marsh signed on and other schools are responding. • The police chief put plate reader commitments in writing: a 14-day retention trial, no livestreaming, monthly audits and a public data-sharing agreement after signing. Also answered in writing: the district confirmed on October 1 that LGBTQIA+ protections are unchanged. What's still open: a formal path and sponsor for the student council, the final weighted grades vote, the city's Nov 17 budget vote on the Axon cameras, a public records request, and questions to the Board about the superintendent's license. How this record works: every email appears as a numbered card (E-001 onward) with sender, recipients and date. Officials' statements are quoted, not paraphrased, and labeled as statements rather than policy. Student names other than Zackary's are removed. Sources and an index are at the back. WHAT HAPPENED, WHY I STARTED & WHY IT MATTERS What Happened, Why I Started & Why It Matters How this started, where things stand, and the words you need to read the rest. What happened Two cases involving former Sun Prairie West High School staff shaped how a lot of students feel about safety and trust in our district. These are the facts as reported in public court records and the news: • Robert Gilkey-Meisegeier, a former coach and dean of students, pleaded guilty in federal court to producing child sexual abuse material. On April 28, 2026, he was sentenced to 18 years in federal prison. A related state case was dismissed after the federal conviction. • Jennifer Ploeger, a former principal, was charged with three misdemeanor counts of failing to report suspected child abuse. On June 25, 2026, she pleaded no contest to one count, the other two were dismissed, and she was placed in a deferred prosecution program. A no contest plea is not an admission of guilt, and she has not been convicted. Students mostly learned about both cases through rumors and the news, not from the district. That gap is a big reason this work exists. Sources: WKOW, Apr 28, 2026 · WTMJ, Jun 1, 2026 · WMTV15, Jun 25, 2026 · Spectrum News, Jun 25, 2026. Status as of October 20, 2026. Why I started In January 2026, I wrote to the Sun Prairie School Board after a hard stretch in our district left a lot of students unsure what happened and who to trust. I proposed a six-part Student Safety & Trust Framework: clearer communication after serious incidents, a plain explanation of how reporting works, the same rules in every building, a real student voice, better mental health support, and regular check-ins on how it's going. That letter turned into meetings with district leaders, a new Student Senate at a district high school, students helping choose a principal and a superintendent, a seat on the weighted grades work group, and a proposal for a district-wide Student Advisory Council. Along the way, the same questions about transparency led to meetings with the Sun Prairie Police Department about its license plate reader cameras. The goal hasn't changed. Student voice should be a regular, documented part of how SPASD makes decisions, not something that depends on one student or one principal. Why it's important Students are the people most affected by what happens in our schools, but we're usually the last to hear about it and the least likely to be asked. When something serious happens and nobody tells us anything, rumors fill the gap. That makes it harder to trust the adults who are supposed to keep us safe, and harder to speak up when something is wrong. WHAT HAPPENED, WHY I STARTED & WHY IT MATTERS In outreach this year, most students said they feel physically safe at school. The problem is follow-through. As one student put it: "Yes I feel safe at school. Yes I would feel comfortable telling an adult. No adults do not listen." Decisions about grades, safety, communication, and leadership shape the next four years of our lives. Weighted grades and Act 95 decide who gets guaranteed admission to UW schools. How incidents are communicated decides whether we hear the truth or a rumor. Who leads our schools decides how all of that gets handled. Students should have a say before those decisions are final, not find out after. It also works when it's done right. Students served on principal and superintendent interview panels, helped restart a Student Senate, shaped the weighted grades plan, and got the district to start sending its newsletters to every student. Those changes happened because students asked, followed up, and kept a record. The same goes beyond school. The license plate reader cameras affect everyone who drives in Sun Prairie, including students and their families. People deserve to know what's being collected, who can see it, and how long it's kept, in plain language. Why this record exists I keep every email, invite, and set of notes so the conversations, answers, and commitments don't get lost, and so anyone can check what was said and when. Student names have been removed, except mine. This is an independent, student-led record, not an official Sun Prairie Area School District document, and it is shared in good faith, not to accuse any person. WHAT HAPPENED, WHY I STARTED & WHY IT MATTERS Glossary • Act 95 — Wisconsin law that guarantees UW admission to top-ranked students, which is why class rank and how GPA is calculated matter. • ALPR — Automated license plate reader: a camera that photographs passing cars and reads the plate. • Axon — The company Sun Prairie plans to switch to for plate readers, starting May 2027. • Capstone — An advanced, project-based course; part of the weighted grades plan. • F-18 — SPPD's written policy on license plate readers. • Flock — Flock Safety, the company behind Sun Prairie's current plate reader cameras. • Fusus — Software that can pull camera feeds into a live view. The Chief said there will be no livestreaming. • Hotlist — A list of plates police are looking for, such as stolen cars. A match is an alert, not proof of a crime. • MOU — Memorandum of understanding: a written agreement between agencies, here about sharing plate data. • PSC — The City of Sun Prairie's Public Safety Committee. • SP-ALPR — Sun Prairie ALPR, Zackary's independent project on the city's plate readers (sunprairiealpr.netlify.app). • SPASD — Sun Prairie Area School District. • SPPD — Sun Prairie Police Department. • SPWHS / SPW — Sun Prairie West High School. SPE is Sun Prairie East. • T&L Committee — The Board of Education's Teaching & Learning Committee. • Weighted grades — A GPA scale where harder classes (AP, capstones, some dual credit) can count up to 5.0 instead of 4.0. • 287(g) — A federal program that lets local agencies help with immigration enforcement. SPPD says plate data won't be shared with agencies in it. • Committee of the Whole — A Board of Education meeting where all members discuss an item in depth before a formal vote. • MTSS — Multi-tiered system of support: a school's layered approach to academic and emotional help, from all students to those needing the most. • Outpost — Axon's solar-powered plate reader camera, the model in the draft Sun Prairie estimate. • Peer Ambassadors — A Patrick Marsh student group whose members may join the student council pilot. • PLC — Professional Learning Center, 220 Kroncke Dr., where the Board of Education meets. • SP30 — Sun Prairie East's daily advisory period, where announcements and slides are shared. • Public records request — A request under Wisconsin law for copies of government records. STUDENT VOICE & DISTRICT ENGAGEMENT • Trust and consistency across schools Sample questions: • "Do you feel students currently have a meaningful voice in district decisions?" • "How would you rate communication to students about important issues?" (1–5 scale) • "Should students have a role in leadership decisions, such as principal or superintendent selection?" • "What specific changes would you like to see moving forward?" (open response) Policy Context: Why Act 95 Matters to Sun Prairie Students The law: Wisconsin Act 95 created the Wisconsin Guarantee and Direct Admit Wisconsin, giving guaranteed admission to University of Wisconsin System schools for top-ranked students in every graduating class. "The sole criterion for ranking pupils shall be the pupil's grade point average." — Wisconsin Act 95 • Top 5% — Guaranteed admission to UW–Madison • Top 10% — Guaranteed admission to all other UW System schools The problem for Sun Prairie: Class rank runs on GPA alone, and SPASD currently ranks students on an unweighted scale. An unweighted "A" in a study hall counts the same as an "A" in AP Calculus or AP Chemistry. Students who challenge themselves in honors and AP courses can be pushed out of the top 5% and 10% by peers with lighter schedules. 31 SPWHS students, including Zackary, organized as the Act 95 group, gathered student voice, and presented a recommendation at the January 26, 2026 Board hearing. Our Ask: A Weighted GPA System for SPASD Give rigor its due weight, so students who take the hardest classes aren't penalized under Act 95 ranking. • 4.0 — Standard scale today: an A is an A, regardless of course difficulty • 29 — SPWHS students organized in the Weighted GPA working group, alongside the Act 95 group • 5%/10% — The Act 95 rank thresholds that decide UW guarantee eligibility What Student Senate is asking the Board to consider: 1. Add weighted points for Honors, AP, and dual-enrollment coursework on the SPASD transcript scale. 2. Model the change against three graduating classes to confirm it doesn't create new inequities. 3. Use the Student Advocacy survey to bring student and family sentiment directly into the board's discussion. Building Relationships: Meeting with District & Building Leadership 1. New Superintendent — Dr. Antoine Reed: Building a working relationship with SPASD's incoming superintendent, who took office July 1, 2026. 2. Board Leadership — Diana McFarland, Board President: Ongoing correspondence since January 2026 on the Safety & Trust Framework and student representation. 2. STUDENT VOICE & DISTRICT ENGAGEMENT E-001 · Student Safety, Trust, and a Proposed Framework for SPASD From Zackary Mark (school account) To Diana Mcfarland <dmmcfar@sunprairieschools.org>, Bryn Horton <bmhorto@sunprairieschools.org>, Colleen Uhlenkamp <cmuhlen@sunprairieschools.org>, Amanda Davis <andavis@sunprairieschools.org>, Melissa Grayson <mjgrays@sunprairieschools.org>, Isaac Sung <cisung@sunprairieschools.org>, Danny Miller <dmille@sunprairieschools.org> Date Jan 13, 2026 Dear Members of the Sun Prairie Area School District Board of Education, I am writing as a follow-up to prior student concerns regarding school climate, safety, and transparency across the Sun Prairie Area School District. I appreciate the time and attention the Board has given to student and family feedback, and I am writing to further clarify the depth of concern being felt by students and to propose a constructive framework for moving forward. As students, we recognize that schools operate within complex legal, personnel, and privacy constraints. At the same time, it is important to communicate that the cumulative effect of multiple incidents across the district—at the elementary, middle, and high school levels—has contributed to an atmosphere of uncertainty and concern among students. These concerns are shaped not only by specific publicly reported cases, but also by the perception that some issues are addressed quietly or without clear communication to the broader school community. Many students have shared that when serious situations arise and little is acknowledged publicly beyond limited statements, it becomes difficult to understand how safety systems are functioning or how future harm is being prevented. This uncertainty affects students’ sense of security and their ability to fully engage in learning. The Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction emphasizes safe, supportive, and inclusive learning environments, as well as continuous improvement through reflection, transparency, and stakeholder engagement. From a student perspective, safety includes not only physical protection, but also trust in reporting systems, confidence in adult accountability, and clarity about how concerns are handled across the district. In the spirit of constructive problem-solving, I respectfully offer the following Student Safety and Trust Framework for the Board’s consideration. This framework is intended to align with DPI guidance while responding to student experiences. First, clear acknowledgment and communication when serious incidents occur. Even when details cannot be shared, district communication that acknowledges impact, explains general processes, and reaffirms safeguards would help reduce speculation and anxiety among students and families. Second, a districtwide safety and reporting overview. Students and families would benefit from a clear, accessible explanation of how concerns are reported, investigated, and resolved, including the roles of school administration, district leadership, and external authorities, when applicable. Transparency about process builds trust without violating privacy. Third, consistent implementation of safety and conduct protocols across all schools. Students notice differences in how similar situations are handled between buildings. A clearly defined, districtwide framework aligned with restorative practices and DPI expectations would promote fairness and accountability. STUDENT VOICE & DISTRICT ENGAGEMENT Student Senate Restart Framework STUDENT SENATE RESTART FRAMEWORK (PHASE I) — Sun Prairie West High School This document outlines a phased relaunch of the Student Senate at Sun Prairie West High School, utilizing a gradual and sustainable model that will begin in April. Phase I focuses on rebuilding systems, establishing credibility, and strengthening student–administration collaboration before expanding to a full representative body. The restart model prioritizes sustainability, consistency, achievable goals, and administrative partnership over immediate scale. I. Purpose The Student Senate exists to provide structured student input on school improvement, policy feedback, and campus climate. During Phase I, the Senate will operate as a small pilot advisory team rather than a full legislative body. II. Core Objectives (Phase I) 1. Re-establish consistent student–administration dialogue. 2. Create repeatable and documented meeting systems. 3. Complete one measurable improvement initiative. 4. Build student awareness and trust in the Senate process. 5. Develop a foundation for gradual expansion in Phase II. 6. Represent diverse student perspectives across grade levels and involvement areas. 7. Provide structured input on school policies, academic systems, and improvement initiatives. 8. Review and respond to student concerns in a systematic and documented manner. 9. Partner with administration in school improvement planning. 10. Promote transparency between students and school leadership. Definition of a Measurable Initiative: A measurable initiative must include: • A clearly defined problem • Documented student input • A written recommendation • A tracked outcome or administrative response III. Authority & Scope The Student Senate holds formal advisory authority in the following areas: • Academic policies (grading feedback, weighted GPA structures, scheduling feedback) • Student climate and equity initiatives • School improvement planning • Student discipline framework feedback Zackary Mark — Advocacy Records 2026 — Complete Edition · v3.0 ↑ Contents Page 69

2. STUDENT VOICE & DISTRICT ENGAGEMENT 1. Make sure everyone is safe and accounted for. 2. Communications works with the principal and district leadership to confirm facts. 3. Decide who is affected, what each audience needs, and what's ready to share. 4. Her team prepares and reviews the message. 5. It comes from the principal, district leadership, or the superintendent, based on severity. 6. More information follows as it's confirmed. What can't be shared, and why: • Names of students involved — student privacy laws; many involve minors • Individual consequences and discipline — protected student records • Grades and other student records — protected student records • Personnel matters — employee protections; directors often don't have the details either Both directors stressed accuracy. Rumors on social media can spread faster than the district can verify facts, and sending wrong information would hurt trust more than a short delay. 04 What students asked for Hear something reliable from the district, even when details can't be shared, because silence gets filled by rumors. • Short, factual messages: even with no names, "a medical incident closed this area, here's what you need to know" takes five minutes and stops rumors. • Name the law: when something can't be shared because of a law, say which one. Many students will look it up. • Trust students' understanding: students often feel information is held back because adults assume they won't get it. Most do. • "You said, we did" updates: follow up on what actually happened, even if it's "nothing changed yet, here's what's happening." 3. WEIGHTED GRADES & ACT 95 Caregiver Survey: Key Findings (October 22, 2026) Released for the public record after Dr. Mould said the findings could be shared (per Zackary, November 10, 2026). Written by Zackary for the weighted grades work group, October 22, 2026, after Dr. Mould asked a student to analyze the caregiver survey. The raw responses are not reproduced here because some families left names and emails for follow-up. The short version 531 caregivers answered in the first week, and 70% support weighted grades. The biggest risk for the plan is timing, not whether to weight. 1. Support is strong and even. 70% rated it a 4 or 5. Support was about the same at West (68%) and East (73%). 2. Timing splits by family. Caregivers of current high schoolers want it applied now, 69% to 31%. Families with only younger kids want to start next year, 74% to 26%. Our Oct 20 plan starts with next year's freshmen, so the families most invested are the ones it leaves out. 3. Rigor is the reason. Supporters say over and over that harder classes should count more. AP is the clear favorite to weight (85%). 4. Opponents worry about fairness and simplicity. The top reasons: all classes have value, keep the 4.0 simple, and students without access to AP fall behind. 5. Families want it explained. 72% asked for a detailed written explanation. Undecided caregivers mostly said they need more information, not that they disagree. Who answered 531 responses came in from Oct 16 to Oct 22, and 62% arrived on the first day (328). • Families with a current high schooler (grades 9–12): 320 • Families with only K–8 students: 204 • Sun Prairie West families: 263 • Sun Prairie East families: 245 • Other or no school listed (virtual, Prairie Phoenix, blank): 23 Families could list more than one grade, so the rows overlap. The East and West counts are close, so neither school's families dominate the results. Support for weighted grades 70% of caregivers support weighted grades, and only 19% oppose them (526 ratings). Support barely changes by group: 68% at West, 73% at East, and 70% for families both with and without a current high schooler. Opposition is strong among the few who hold it: most opponents chose 1, not 2. Zackary Mark — Advocacy Records 2026 — Complete Edition · v3.0 ↑ Contents Page 153

WEIGHTED GRADES & ACT 95 When it should start Overall it's close to a tie, but the split by family is large (462 clear timing answers): families with a current high schooler want it now, and families with younger kids want to wait. Each group mostly picked the option that helps their own child. That's normal, but it means the families with the most at stake are the ones our plan leaves out. 61 caregivers skipped this question, mostly people who oppose weighting entirely. Which classes, and why AP is the clear favorite: 85% want AP weighted. That matches our recommendation. • Classes to weight: AP 85% · dual enrollment 46% · STEM Academy 17% • Factors they weighed: rigor 75% · college credit 57% · time commitment 56% • How they want to learn about it: detailed written explanation 72% · information sessions 40% The course list in our export is cut off, so options listed after STEM (including capstones) can't be counted. The full spreadsheet would fix that. Rigor beating college credit supports our choice to weight capstones, not only classes that earn credit. What families wrote 388 caregivers explained their rating. Supporters mostly talk about effort, while opponents talk about fairness. Quotes are anonymous and copied as written. • Support (4–5), 276 explained: harder classes should count more (about half name rigor, effort or AP); Act 95 and direct admit; other districts already do it; the current system discourages AP. "Harder schedules should be rewarded." · "Extra incentive to take advanced classes" · "This is long overdue!" • Unsure (3), 41 explained: need more information; want the pros, cons and reasoning first. "Need more information. Pros and cons." · "Hate to pressure students" • Oppose (1–2), 70 explained: all classes have equal value; keep the 4.0 simple; equity for students without AP access; stress; colleges recalculate GPA anyway. "Every class should have equal importance." · "The scale stops at 4 for a reason." · "It's not equitable" A warning sign about the survey itself: a few opponents said it reads as if the decision is already made. The timing question had no "don't adopt it" option, and 44 caregivers who rated it a 1 skipped that question. The communication package should show that feedback can still change the plan. Questions families want answered 147 caregivers left a comment or question. These five came up most and belong in the communication package's FAQ. 1. Does it apply to my student, and when does it start? The most common question (about 23 comments), often about a current junior or senior. Some asked whether GPAs would be recalculated going back. 2. How does it affect Act 95 and college admissions? Families asked how it ties to the Wisconsin guarantee and whether colleges use the weighted GPA. 3. WEIGHTED GRADES & ACT 95 3. Which classes count? People asked about audition music classes, electives, dual credit and capstones. Some said college credit alone shouldn't earn a weight. 4. Is it fair to students without access? Families asked whether every student can get into weighted classes. 5. Why change now, and is it already decided? A few wanted the reasons behind the change and proof the survey matters. Recommendations for the work group • Oct 27 (work group): decide how we answer families of current high schoolers before anything goes public. Option A: keep "next year's freshmen only" and give a short, honest reason, for example that current students chose classes under the old rules and changing them mid-course isn't fair. Option B: weight classes taken from 2027–28 on for every student, without recalculating past grades. Either way, say plainly that past grades won't be recalculated. • One-page communication package: lead with the reason (rigor), list exactly which classes count, and add a five-question FAQ built from the section above. 72% asked for a written explanation, so the written piece matters more than events. • Nov 2 and Nov 9 (Board): bring three numbers: 70% caregiver support, 78% of students choosing a weighted option in the Act 95 survey, and the 69% to 31% timing split. Name the split ourselves rather than letting Board members hear it first from parents. • Address equity directly. Opponents' strongest point is access. Show how students get into AP and capstone classes and what support exists, so weighting doesn't look like a reward only for students who already have access. Method and limits • Source: the PDF export of the caregiver survey responses (531 rows, Oct 16–22). 4. DISTRICT BUDGET Explainer: How the SPASD Budget Works One-page explainer published on the SPASD Student Voice website, from the August 18, 2026 meeting with the Director of Business & Finance. The short version: the district's money mostly pays for people, the amount it gets depends on how many students enroll, and Wisconsin's per-student funding hasn't kept up with inflation. • Biggest cost: about 80% of spending is staff. The rest covers busing, supplies, and utilities. • Revenue: driven by enrollment through state formulas. Revenue must equal expenses. • Budget calendar: built over 8–9 months, starting in February, adopted in October. • Long-term plan: a 5-year forecast is updated every February. • 2024 referendum: $25 million passed; about $7 million went to staff pay after a wage study. • Savings: fund balance is about 21%. Around 15–20% is considered healthy. • Federal Title grants: about $160,000 less than last year. These fund the highest-need schools. • Special education: the state covers roughly 30% of actual cost; general funds cover the rest. The most common misunderstanding: many people assume more state aid means more money for schools. Under Wisconsin's revenue limit, the district can only collect a set amount. More state aid mostly lowers the local property tax levy instead of raising the total. Biggest risks ahead: • Per-student funding not tied to inflation • Enrollment projected to decline, partly due to housing costs • Possible operating deficit down the road as costs rise How to follow along: • Watch Board of Education meetings and the annual public budget meeting each fall • Talk to the student representatives on the Board • Tell state lawmakers how school funding affects your school Zackary Mark — Advocacy Records 2026 — Complete Edition · v3.0 ↑ Contents Page 167

History: Replaces F-18 (12/17/2010); updated 08/11/2014, 10/31/2016, new format 05/06/2025, updated 3/03/2026. 2598 West Main Street, Sun Prairie, WI 53590. 1.1 Policy The Sun Prairie Police Department (SNPD) utilizes Automated License Plate Readers (ALPR) to enhance public safety, aid in criminal investigations, and improve law enforcement efficiency. ALPR capture infrared images of vehicle license plates, convert them to digital text using Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology, and match them against databases of license plates of interest. ALPR can alert officers when a match is detected, aiding in identifying stolen vehicles, wanted persons, and other subjects of interest. This policy governs the use, management, and retention of ALPR data by SNPD personnel, ensuring compliance with privacy laws and safeguarding civil liberties. 1.2 Objective To provide department members with guidelines on the proper use of the ALPR in their official duties. 1.3 Definitions • ALPR (Automated License Plate Reader): A system consisting of cameras and technology that captures images of vehicle license plates, converts them to digital text using OCR, and compares them to databases of vehicles of interest. • OCR (Optical Character Recognition): Technology that identifies printed characters using photoelectric devices and computer software. • Read: A digital image of a license plate and associated metadata (e.g., date, time, and geographic coordinates) captured by the ALPR system. • Alert: A visual and/or auditory notice triggered when an ALPR system detects a match between a scanned license plate and a plate of interest in the system's database. • Hit: A read that matches a license plate on a list of plates related to stolen vehicles, wanted individuals, or other investigatory purposes. • Hot List: A list of license plate numbers of interest to law enforcement agencies, including, but not limited to, stolen cars, vehicles owned by persons of interest, and vehicles associated with AMBER Alerts. Hot list information can come from a variety of sources, including the National Insurance Crime Bureau and the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), national AMBER Alerts and Department of Homeland Security watch lists. The Department of Transportation can provide lists of expired registration plates, and agencies can interface their own locally compiled hot lists. These lists serve an officer safety function as well as an investigatory purpose. • Stored ALPR Data: Data, including license plate images, vehicle images, and metadata, obtained by the ALPR system and stored for future querying. Highlighting is from the original. Part of the page break between the two sheets was not photographed. 09/23/26 Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism hearing • 13 principles released by national law enforcement and public safety organizations (International Association of Chiefs of Police, National Sheriff's Organization, National District Attorneys Association, National Fusion Center Association, and National High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas, and more) • Sun Prairie Police Department currently follows all 13 principles. • Written policies. Every law enforcement agency using ALPR systems must adopt and enforce clear written policies governing authorized uses, access, documented queries, verification, retention, sharing, data security, auditing, and accountability. • Permitted uses. ALPR must be used by trained and authorized law enforcement personnel only for legitimate law enforcement and public safety purposes. • Authorized access. System access must be subject to strong controls, routine auditing, and accountability for misuse—and promptly removed when an individual's duties no longer require it. • Auditing and accountability. Agencies must maintain access logs, conduct routine audits, and investigate potential misuse. Policy violations shall result in meaningful discipline, up to and including termination, consistent with applicable due process requirements. Suspected criminal misuse must be referred to the appropriate authorities for investigation and potential prosecution under applicable law. • Required training. Personnel with access to ALPR information shall receive initial and ongoing training on permitted uses, verification requirements, privacy and security protections, and the consequences of misuse. • Documented queries. ALPR queries must be tied to an official case number or another documented law enforcement or public safety purpose, with query and access logs maintained for auditing and accountability. • Verification of plate matches. ALPR information must be appropriately verified before enforcement action is taken. An alert alone does not identify the driver, establish guilt, or replace other investigative work. • Confidentiality. ALPR data collected for law enforcement purposes must remain appropriately protected from public disclosure. Comparable protections must apply when a private company stores or manages the information on behalf of a government agency. • Meaningful retention. Retention policies must preserve information needed for legitimate investigations while protecting privacy and security. The significance of a vehicle may not become apparent until weeks or months after a crime, particularly when a victim's report is delayed or an investigation develops over time. Strong access controls, documented queries, and auditing are more effective safeguards against misuse than destroying potentially important investigative information after an arbitrarily short time Zackary Mark — Advocacy Records 2026 — Complete Edition · v3.0 ↑ Contents Page 227

Law enforcement must be able to responsibly share and query ALPR information across jurisdictions because missing people, victims, dangerous offenders, and criminal activity do not stop at jurisdictional boundaries. Sharing by agencies must be limited to legitimate law enforcement and public safety purposes and subject to appropriate controls and oversight. Government agencies must not sell access to ALPR data they collect. • Law enforcement access to non-governmental ALPR data. The same restrictions, safeguards, and accountability requirements must apply to law enforcement's access to and use of ALPR data regardless of whether the data was collected by a government agency, a commercial provider, or another non-governmental entity. • Data security. Law enforcement agencies, technology providers, and other entities that store or manage ALPR information must maintain strong security, access, and disclosure protections. Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) Technology: Frequently Asked Questions The Sun Prairie Police Department (SNPD) is committed to using technology responsibly to enhance public safety while respecting the privacy and rights of our community members. As the department transitions from Flock Safety to Axon automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology, we recognize that residents may have questions about how the system works, what information is collected, who can access it, and how that information is protected. The following frequently asked questions explain the technology, its intended use, and the safeguards in place to promote transparency, accountability, and responsible data management. Understanding the Technology What is an Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR)? An Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) is a camera-based technology that captures images of vehicles and their license plates as they pass a specific location. ALPR technology provides law enforcement with an additional investigative tool to help identify vehicles associated with criminal activity, locate missing persons, and support other legitimate public safety investigations. The cameras capture information at a specific point in time. They do not provide continuous, real-time tracking of vehicles or individuals. What information do ALPR cameras collect? The Axon ALPR system captures: • An image of the vehicle's license plate. • A broader image of the vehicle and its surroundings. • Basic visible vehicle characteristics, such as color, make, and vehicle type. • The date, time, and location where the vehicle was photographed. Because the cameras capture images of the surrounding area, photographs may incidentally include nearby people, signs, buildings, or other objects. However, the system does not use facial recognition technology or analyze images to identify pedestrians or vehicle occupants. United States (1967), the United States Supreme Court established the "reasonable expectation of privacy" test and held that what an individual knowingly exposes to the public is generally not protected by the Fourth Amendment. In United States v. Knotts (1983), the Court further held that "a person traveling in an automobile on public thoroughfares has no reasonable expectation of privacy in his movements from one place to another," as those movements are voluntarily exposed to public observation. Similarly, in New York v. Class (1986), the Court found that individuals do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy in information that is required by law to be displayed on a vehicle and visible to the public, such as a Vehicle Identification Number (VIN). This same rationale has been applied by courts to license plates displayed on public roads. More recently, courts reviewing Automated License Plate Reader technology have generally concluded that the capture of a license plate and vehicle image at a point in time, visible to anyone traveling on a public roadway, does not by itself constitute an unreasonable search under the Fourth Amendment. Weighted Grades: What Families Need to Know (student draft for the work group) A short explainer drafted by a student member of the SPASD weighted grades work group, October 2026. This is a recommendation. The School Board makes the final decision. What's changing: right now, SPASD uses an unweighted 4.0 GPA, so an A counts the same in every class. The work group is recommending a 5.0 scale for the most challenging classes. In a weighted class, an A would count as 5.0 instead of 4.0. Which classes would be weighted (5.0 scale): • AP courses • Capstone classes, including try-out music courses • Classes that earn college credit or an industry certification Not weighted: • College-credit or certification classes that match a class the high school already offers • Classes that don't transfer for credit to UW colleges and universities Counselors are reviewing the Madison College class list now. Every weighted class will be marked in the course guide so students know before they choose. Who it applies to: the recommendation is to start with students entering 9th grade in fall 2027 (the Class of 2031) and add a grade each year after that. Why not current students? Current high schoolers chose their classes under the old rules. Changing the rules partway through would reward some choices after the fact and not others, and it would change class rank for students who are already being ranked. Starting with a new class means every student in it knows the rules before choosing a single course. Open question for the work group: 69% of caregivers of current high schoolers asked for it to apply now. One option to consider is weighting classes taken from 2027–28 onward for every student, without recalculating past grades. Questions families asked: • Does it apply to my student? Under the recommendation, only to students starting 9th grade in fall 2027 or later. • Will past grades be recalculated? No. Grades already earned stay as they are. • How does it connect to Act 95 and college? Act 95 guarantees admission to Universities of Wisconsin schools for students in the top 10% of their class (top 5% for UW–Madison), so class rank matters. How to Start Student Voice at Your School (a guide for any student) 1. Start with one clear letter. Write to your principal or School Board about one thing students are worried about. Say what happened, how it affects students, and two or three specific, doable asks. Keep it respectful. You're asking to be part of the solution, not blaming anyone. 2. Ask for a meeting, then write it down. Ask for 30 minutes. Bring a one-page handout. Take notes, and ask before recording. Within two days, email a short recap ("so we all leave with the same notes"). That recap is what turns a nice conversation into a commitment. 3. Get real input, not just your friends'. Run a short anonymous survey in every language families speak. Share it through teachers and newsletters, not only social media. Report who answered, including who's missing. 4. Keep a public record. Post short updates: what you asked, what you were told, what changed. A free website and an Instagram account are enough. Give district leaders a chance to correct anything before you post it, and set a deadline. 5. Track promises. Keep a "You said, we did" list. Every commitment gets an owner, a date and a status. Celebrate wins publicly; it's the best proof that speaking up works. 6. Join the groups that already exist. Work groups, Student Senate and Board student sessions are where decisions get made. Ask to join them before starting something new. 7. Protect people. Don't post names of students, private phone numbers, or rumors about staff. Stick to facts from public records and the news. If someone tells you they're unsafe, help them reach a trusted adult right away. 8. Make it last after you graduate. Recruit co-leads from different grades and schools early. 10. GET INVOLVED How to Speak Up How any student or family member can do what's in this record. Email a district leader 1. Find the right person. The Who's who page and the district website list roles. 2. Keep it short: who you are, what you're asking, and one clear question. 3. Ask for something specific: an answer, a meeting, or a document. 4. If there's no reply after a week, follow up once, politely. Speak at a Board of Education meeting 1. Check the posted agenda on BoardDocs (go.boarddocs.com/wi/spasd/Board.nsf). 2. Sign up for public comment the way the agenda describes, usually before the meeting starts. 3. Plan for about three minutes. Say your name, your school, your point and one ask. 4. Bring a written copy to hand in. Talk to the Board's student representatives They serve two-year terms, from the end of sophomore year through senior year. Recruiting starts in December and applications open in mid-January. You can reach the current reps any time. Ask the city for public records Wisconsin's public records law lets anyone ask for government records. Police records go through the city's online records portal; other city records go to the City Clerk. Describe exactly what you want and the date range. Comment on a city decision Email the Mayor and the committee, speak during public comment in Council Chambers at 300 E. Main St., or ask your alder where they stand. The City Clerk's office can tell you how to sign up. Zackary Mark — Advocacy Records 2026 — Complete Edition · v3.0 ↑ Contents Page 322

ABOUT ME What I Learned (draft for Zackary to approve) Draft for Zackary to edit. Written from his own words in the district's Nov 3 article and his emails. "When I first started this, I didn't have that confidence. I've grown that, but you have to be able to send an email. Like, that's basic stuff, and then you gradually go from there." That's what I told the district in October, for its Nov 3 feature, and it's still true. The biggest thing I learned is that follow-through matters more than the first ask. Most of what changed this year happened because someone wrote back, and then I wrote back again. The newsletter commitment, the weighted grades plan, and the student council all started as one email and turned into a conversation. I also learned to keep a record. "The district said this, that they're gonna do this. Now here's the evidence that they did this." That's why this archive exists. It's about building trust, and trust needs receipts. Not every answer was yes. Some people said a group like this wasn't their call, or that they needed approval first. That's fair, and it taught me to find the right person and the right process instead of pushing harder at the wrong door. If you're a student thinking about speaking up, start at your comfort level. Write the email. Then make the call. Then go to the meeting. You build confidence one step at a time. Zackary Mark — Advocacy Records 2026 — Complete Edition · v3.0 ↑ Contents Page 341
